 By Legis1 Editorial · Edited by Matthew Dougherty, Joanne Levine Saturday, November 21, 2026 · 2 min read Why It Matters
 The Agriculture Department's Nov. 10 proposed rule would implement provisions of the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, expanding SNAP work requirements and restricting states' ability to obtain geographic waivers. ​ 
 For lobbyists representing state governments, anti-hunger organizations and affected communities, the proposal raises urgent questions about eligibility, administrative costs and potential benefit losses.
 More Americans Could Lose SNAP Benefits
 The proposal would extend SNAP's three-month time limit to adults ages 55 through 64 and lower the dependent-child exception from under 18 to under 14. It would eliminate exceptions for homeless individuals, veterans, and former foster care youth while adding exceptions for Indians, Urban Indians, and California Indians.
 States would also face stricter waiver requirements. The proposal would eliminate the insufficient-jobs criterion, generally require unemployment above 10%, and prohibit combining multiple geographic areas to qualify. These changes to 7 CFR 271.2 and 7 CFR 273.24 could substantially affect SNAP eligibility and state administration.
 The Divide
 Republicans have defended the underlying legislation. Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR) praised its work requirements, while Rep. Erin Houchin (R-IN) argued the law restored them.
 Democrats have warned about benefit losses. Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) cited potential SNAP reductions of $310 billion in May 2025 floor remarks . Rep. Jim Costa (D-CA) said in July 2026 that more than 700,000 children had already lost benefits across 12 reporting states.

 These statements concern the underlying law, not the proposed rule. Explore other congressional statements on Legis1 .
 Congressional Hearings Reveal Competing Priorities
 Congress examined SNAP work requirements and administration in three relevant hearings:
 April 8, 2025 : The Power of Work: Expanding Opportunity Through SNAP. 
 Sept. 9, 2025 : Exploring State Options in SNAP. 
 June 25, 2026 : Combating Waste, Fraud, and Abuse in SNAP. 
 The latest hearing featured witnesses from USDA, Advancing American Freedom, and the Food Research and Action Center, among others. None specifically addressed the November proposal.
 Read the hearing records on Legis1 to identify arguments relevant to congressional outreach.
 Two Lobbying Disclosures Reveal SNAP Policy Interests
 Federal lobbying disclosures show that major corporations and local governments have raised SNAP-related issues.
 Unilever U.S. Inc. reported $540,000 in first-quarter lobbying expenditures, with "SNAP Waivers" listed among its lobbying issues.
 Mecklenburg County, North Carolina , reported $20,000 in third-quarter lobbying expenditures, identifying SNAP administrative costs and eligibility requirement changes among its issues.
 These amounts represent total expenditures reported on filings mentioning SNAP-related issues, not spending exclusively on the proposed rule.
 Which other organizations have disclosed SNAP lobbying activity, and what specific policies have they sought to influence? Investigate additional lobbying disclosures on Legis1 .
 December 10 Is the Deadline
 USDA is seeking comments on implementing new exceptions for Indian populations and potential alignment with Medicaid requirements. Comments are due Dec. 10 . The proposal lists docket FNA-2025-0368 and RIN 0584-AF09. Filers should verify the docket association before using the Regulations.gov submission link .
